projects.name: iDynamics
projects.title: Making dynamic systems experiments reproducible.
projects.summary: A configurable emulation framework for evaluating microservice scheduling policies under controllable cloud–edge dynamics.
projects.paper_title: iDynamics: A Configurable Emulation Framework for Evaluating Microservice Scheduling Policies under Controllable Cloud–Edge Dynamics
projects.authors: Ming Chen, Muhammed Tawfiqul Islam, Maria Rodriguez Read, and Rajkumar Buyya
projects.problem: A scheduling policy can look effective under one workload and struggle when traffic, network conditions, or application behavior changes. Comparing policies requires a way to control those changes and repeat the experiment.
projects.contribution: I developed a configurable framework that connects workload generation, evolving service call graphs, network emulation, and policy evaluation. The implementation uses aggregate Prometheus queries and sparse graph construction, with distributed network verification and per-run evidence records.
decisions: Make dynamics configurable
Represent workload and network changes as experimental inputs so that the same scenario can be replayed across scheduling policies.
Connect application and infrastructure views
Use service-level telemetry and call-graph information together with node-level network conditions to describe the environment a scheduler actually sees.
Evaluate the emulation itself
Measure how closely configured delay and bandwidth match observed behavior, alongside the effect of scheduling decisions.
projects.result: The framework was evaluated on a research testbed with one control-plane node and 45 workers. Delay-injection validation across 72 directed pairs in a nine-worker subset reported a mean absolute error of 0.274 ms. Mean relative bandwidth-shaping error was 4.28% in the reported validation.
projects.limitation: Emulation offers controlled conditions for comparing policies. Its results still depend on the selected applications, hardware, workloads, and configured dynamics; evaluation in another deployment requires fresh measurements.
projects.metric_label: worker nodes in the evaluation testbed

projects.name: TraDE
projects.title: Placing microservices with traffic and network conditions in view.
projects.summary: Network- and traffic-aware adaptive scheduling for microservices operating under changing conditions.
projects.paper_title: TraDE: Network and Traffic-Aware Adaptive Scheduling for Microservices Under Dynamics
projects.authors: Ming Chen, Muhammed Tawfiqul Islam, Maria Rodriguez Read, and Rajkumar Buyya
projects.problem: Microservice response time depends on how much services communicate and the network paths between their hosts. Workload and network changes can make an initially reasonable placement expensive.
projects.contribution: I developed an adaptive scheduling approach that brings measured inter-service traffic and node-to-node network delay into placement decisions, subject to resource constraints.
decisions: Model communication in both directions
Request and response traffic may be asymmetric. Treating both directions explicitly gives the placement objective a more useful picture of communication cost.
Adapt to observed service performance
Use response-time behavior to identify when the current placement needs reconsideration, then evaluate feasible scheduling changes.
Keep placement decisions executable
Connect the scheduling algorithm to Kubernetes deployment controls and validate its effects with application-level performance measurements.
projects.result: In the evaluated DeathStarBench Social Network scenarios on a ten-node Kubernetes cluster, TraDE reports up to 48.3% lower average response time than NetMARKS under changing request patterns and controlled node delays. This is the largest improvement in the tested scenarios, rather than an expected result for every deployment.
projects.limitation: Moving services also has a cost. Placement benefits depend on traffic measurements, the duration of network changes, available capacity, and the operational effect of migration.
projects.metric_label: maximum reduction in average response time vs. NetMARKS

projects.name: AgentFAIR
projects.title: Structured dataset evaluation through collaborative agents.
projects.summary: A multi-agent workflow for evaluating the findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability of geospatial datasets.
projects.paper_title: AgentFAIR: A Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework for FAIRness Evaluation of Geospatial Datasets
projects.problem: FAIRness assessment involves interpreting metadata, checking evidence, and applying criteria consistently across heterogeneous geospatial datasets. Repeating that work manually is time-consuming.
projects.contribution: As co-first and corresponding author, I worked with a supervised student on a multi-agent approach to structured FAIRness evaluation. The implementation connects metadata extraction, 13 FAIR sub-principle evaluators, and critic feedback loops through a LangGraph workflow, with a FastAPI service and a React dashboard.
decisions: Organize around explicit criteria
Separate the dimensions of findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability so that an assessment can be understood criterion by criterion.
Keep the evidence visible
Treat an assessment as a structured evaluation with supporting observations, rather than only a fluent explanation.
Make evaluation part of the workflow
Examine the behavior of the assessment process itself, including consistency and the interpretation of dataset metadata.
projects.result: The public research implementation includes a multi-agent workflow and an interactive evaluation dashboard. The linked preprint presents the methodology and evaluation; the archived software record provides an additional release reference.
projects.limitation: An agent-generated assessment depends on available metadata, access to evidence, the chosen criteria, and model behavior. The public repository does not include every benchmark artifact needed to reproduce all manuscript results.
projects.screenshot_caption: An example assessment shown in the public AgentFAIR dashboard. The displayed FAIR score describes that example dataset; it is not a measure of model accuracy.

projects.name: EN-Beats
projects.title: Forecasting multiple cloud resources with ensemble learning.
projects.summary: An ensemble learning method for multiple-resource prediction in cloud computing environments.
projects.paper_title: EN-Beats: A Novel Ensemble Learning-Based Method for Multiple Resource Predictions in Cloud
projects.authors: Ming Chen, Maria Rodriguez Read, Patricia Arroba, and Rajkumar Buyya
projects.problem: Cloud resource demand changes over time, and different resource signals can exhibit different patterns. Resource management benefits from anticipating demand before making scaling or placement decisions.
projects.contribution: I developed an ensemble learning approach for predicting multiple cloud resource demands, connecting time-series modeling with the needs of resource management.
decisions: Forecast across resource signals
Study multiple resource demands so that a prediction workflow can support decisions beyond a single utilization series.
Use ensemble learning
Combine predictive modeling choices to address variation in resource behavior across the evaluated datasets.
Connect prediction to system decisions
Treat forecasts as inputs to resource management, where evaluation must account for both prediction quality and the downstream use of the estimate.
projects.result: The IEEE CLOUD 2023 evaluation uses Bitbrains resource traces and a ten-minute forecasting horizon. Reported CPU NRMSE is 4.4%, compared with 5.84% for N-BEATS; memory NRMSE is 5.93%, compared with 8.22%. Results vary by resource and metric.
projects.limitation: Forecasting quality is sensitive to the workload, prediction horizon, available history, and shifts in behavior. A deployment should validate the model against its own resource traces.
projects.metric_label: forecasting horizon in the evaluated resource traces

engineering_study.title: Reproducible Transformer training
engineering_study.summary: A controlled training study that connects model design, optimizer behavior, configuration validation, and numerical reproducibility.
engineering_study.scope: Experiments followed the assessment’s seven-epoch budget, fixed seed, dataset split, and evaluation procedure. Validation was reused during development; comparisons describe the development study.
engineering_study.contribution: Implemented and evaluated a modular Transformer training pipeline, with pinned input identities, typed configuration, traceable experiment records, and numerical and protocol checks.
components: Rotary embeddings, SwiGLU layers, and per-head attention gates.
Make architecture changes explicit and comparable.
Separate Muon/AdamW updates with checked parameter routing.
Keep the relationship between parameter groups and updates inspectable.
Fixed protocol, pinned input hashes, typed configuration, and recorded settings.
Connect each result to the code and inputs that produced it.
Evaluation-invariant tests, gradient checks, and CPU/CUDA comparisons.
Find implementation errors and document device-dependent numerical behavior.
engineering_study.outcome: Completed 197 seven-epoch experiments and verified reproduction of the selected CUDA model, optimizer, and scheduler states. Documented numerical differences on CPU.
engineering_study.boundary: This is an engineering assessment study. The validation set was used during development, so the results are not an independent test-set estimate.
